# About these notes

These are my practice notes from class and home. I used small examples to practise R packages, basic programming, graphs, the `apply()` family, linear regression and debugging.

The code is shown in the report. When I knit this file in RStudio, the results and graphs are displayed below the relevant code.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

# 1. Packages

I first check whether the packages are installed. `install.packages()` installs a package, while `library()` loads it into the current R session.

```{r packages}
packages <- c("ggplot2", "dplyr", "readr")
missing <- packages[!packages %in% rownames(installed.packages())]

if (length(missing) > 0) {
  install.packages(missing)
}

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)

"Packages loaded"
```

# 2. Basic R practice

## 2.1 Variables and data types

The assignment operator `<-` stores a value in an object. I used `class()` to check the data type.

```{r variables}
student <- "Prince"
age <- 28
passed <- TRUE

print(student)
print(age)
print(passed)

class(student)
class(age)
class(passed)
```

## 2.2 Vectors and summary functions

`c()` combines values into a vector. I used summary functions to calculate the total, average, median, highest and lowest marks.

```{r vectors}
marks <- c(65, 70, 80, 90, 75)

marks
length(marks)
sum(marks)
mean(marks)
median(marks)
max(marks)
min(marks)
```

## 2.3 Sequences and repetition

The colon operator creates a sequence. `seq()` lets me set the interval, and `rep()` repeats values.

```{r sequences}
numbers <- 1:10
numbers

even_numbers <- seq(2, 20, by = 2)
even_numbers

repeated_values <- rep(5, times = 4)
repeated_values
```

## 2.4 Arithmetic operators

```{r arithmetic}
a <- 20
b <- 5

a + b   # Addition
a - b   # Subtraction
a * b   # Multiplication
a / b   # Division
a %% b  # Remainder
a ^ 2   # Power
```

## 2.5 if / else

The condition is checked first. If the score is at least 50, the result is Pass; otherwise, it is Fail.

```{r if-else}
score <- 65

if (score >= 50) {
  print("Pass")
} else {
  print("Fail")
}
```

## 2.6 Multiple conditions

I used `else if` to check more than two possible grades.

```{r grades}
score <- 78

if (score >= 80) {
  grade <- "A"
} else if (score >= 70) {
  grade <- "B"
} else if (score >= 60) {
  grade <- "C"
} else if (score >= 50) {
  grade <- "D"
} else {
  grade <- "F"
}

grade
```

## 2.7 for loop

A `for` loop repeats the code for each value in a sequence.

```{r for-loop}
for (i in 1:5) {
  print(i)
}
```

## 2.8 while loop

A `while` loop runs as long as its condition is TRUE. I increase the counter so that the loop eventually stops.

```{r while-loop}
counter <- 1

while (counter <= 5) {
  print(counter)
  counter <- counter + 1
}
```

## 2.9 My own function

I wrote a small function to calculate an average. The input is `x`, and `return()` sends the result back.

```{r function}
calculate_average <- function(x) {
  result <- mean(x)
  return(result)
}

calculate_average(c(10, 20, 30, 40))
```

## 2.10 Data frames

A data frame stores data in rows and columns. I used `head()`, `str()` and `summary()` to inspect it.

```{r data-frame}
students <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Aline", "Eric", "Jean", "Diane", "Peter"),
  Age = c(21, 22, 20, 23, 21),
  Marks = c(75, 60, 88, 45, 92)
)

students
head(students)
str(students)
summary(students)
```

# 3. ggplot2 - different geoms

I use `ggplot()` to select the data and `aes()` to connect variables to graph features. The `geom_*()` function determines the type of graph.

```{r create-plot-data}
df <- data.frame(
  Student = c("Aline", "Eric", "Jean", "Diane", "Peter"),
  Gender = c("Female", "Male", "Male", "Female", "Male"),
  Marks = c(75, 60, 88, 45, 92),
  Study_Hours = c(4, 3, 6, 2, 7)
)

df
```

## 3.1 geom_bar()

`geom_bar()` counts the observations in each category. Here I count the students by gender.

```{r geom-bar, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(df, aes(x = Gender)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Students by Gender",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Number of Students"
  )
```

## 3.2 geom_col()

`geom_col()` uses values already in the data. Here, each bar shows a student's mark. The main difference is that `geom_bar()` counts by default, while `geom_col()` uses the supplied y-values.

```{r geom-col, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(df, aes(x = Student, y = Marks)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkgreen") +
  labs(
    title = "Marks by Student",
    x = "Student",
    y = "Marks"
  )
```

## 3.3 geom_histogram()

A histogram shows the distribution of numeric values. `binwidth = 10` groups marks into intervals of 10.

```{r geom-histogram, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(df, aes(x = Marks)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, fill = "orange", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Marks",
    x = "Marks",
    y = "Frequency"
  )
```

## 3.4 geom_boxplot()

A boxplot shows the median, spread and possible outliers. I used it to compare marks by gender.

```{r geom-boxplot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(df, aes(x = Gender, y = Marks)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Marks by Gender",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Marks"
  )
```

## 3.5 geom_point()

A scatter plot displays the relationship between two numeric variables. Each point represents one student.

```{r geom-point, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(df, aes(x = Study_Hours, y = Marks)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Study Hours and Marks",
    x = "Study Hours",
    y = "Marks"
  )
```

## 3.6 geom_line()

A line graph is useful for showing a trend over an ordered variable, such as month.

```{r geom-line, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
monthly <- data.frame(
  Month = 1:6,
  Sales = c(120, 150, 135, 180, 200, 220)
)

ggplot(monthly, aes(x = Month, y = Sales)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "blue") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly Sales",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Sales"
  )
```

## 3.7 geom_smooth()

`geom_smooth()` adds a trend line. `method = "lm"` uses a linear model, and `se = TRUE` displays the confidence band.

```{r geom-smooth, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(df, aes(x = Study_Hours, y = Marks)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Study Hours and Marks - Trend",
    x = "Study Hours",
    y = "Marks"
  )
```

**My notes:** `geom_bar()` counts; `geom_col()` uses given values; histogram shows distribution; boxplot shows spread; point shows a relationship; line shows a trend; smooth adds a fitted trend.

# 4. apply() family

I practised these functions to perform calculations on rows, columns, lists and groups.

| Function | What I use it for |
|---|---|
| `apply()` | Apply a function to matrix rows or columns |
| `lapply()` | Apply a function to each list element; returns a list |
| `sapply()` | Similar to `lapply()`, but tries to simplify the result |
| `vapply()` | Apply a function with an expected output type |
| `tapply()` | Apply a function to groups |
| `mapply()` | Apply a function to multiple inputs |

## 4.1 Create a matrix

```{r matrix}
scores <- matrix(
  c(
    70, 80, 90,
    60, 75, 85,
    88, 92, 95
  ),
  nrow = 3,
  byrow = TRUE
)

colnames(scores) <- c("Math", "English", "Science")
rownames(scores) <- c("Student1", "Student2", "Student3")
scores
```

## 4.2 apply()

`MARGIN = 1` means rows, and `MARGIN = 2` means columns. I calculated averages and totals.

```{r apply}
row_averages <- apply(scores, MARGIN = 1, FUN = mean)
column_averages <- apply(scores, MARGIN = 2, FUN = mean)

row_averages
column_averages

row_totals <- apply(scores, 1, sum)
column_totals <- apply(scores, 2, sum)

row_totals
column_totals
```

## 4.3 lapply()

`lapply()` applies a function to each list element and returns a list.

```{r lapply}
my_list <- list(
  numbers = c(2, 4, 6),
  marks = c(60, 70, 80),
  ages = c(20, 21, 22)
)

list_means <- lapply(my_list, mean)
list_means
```

## 4.4 sapply()

`sapply()` performs a similar calculation but tries to simplify the result.

```{r sapply}
simplified_means <- sapply(my_list, mean)
simplified_means
```

## 4.5 vapply()

`numeric(1)` tells R that I expect one numeric result for each list element.

```{r vapply}
checked_means <- vapply(
  my_list,
  mean,
  FUN.VALUE = numeric(1)
)

checked_means
```

## 4.6 tapply()

`tapply()` calculates a result for each group. Here I calculate the average mark for each gender.

```{r tapply}
student_marks <- c(70, 80, 65, 90, 75, 85)
gender <- c("Female", "Male", "Female", "Male", "Female", "Male")

average_by_gender <- tapply(student_marks, gender, mean)
average_by_gender
```

## 4.7 mapply()

`mapply()` applies a function to corresponding elements from multiple inputs.

```{r mapply}
result_mapply <- mapply(
  FUN = sum,
  x = list(c(1, 2), c(3, 4), c(5, 6)),
  y = list(c(10, 20), c(30, 40), c(50, 60))
)

result_mapply
```

# 5. Linear regression

I used sample data to practise `lm()`, `summary()`, `predict()` and regression diagnostic plots.

- Simple regression uses one predictor.
- Multiple regression uses two or more predictors.
- `Marks` is the response variable I want to predict.

## 5.1 Prepare and inspect the data

```{r regression-data}
regression_data <- data.frame(
  Study_Hours = 1:10,
  Marks = c(42, 48, 51, 57, 61, 68, 72, 78, 84, 89),
  Attendance = c(60, 65, 70, 72, 75, 80, 82, 88, 90, 95)
)

head(regression_data)
summary(regression_data)
str(regression_data)
```

## 5.2 Simple linear regression

The formula `Marks ~ Study_Hours` means that I am predicting Marks using Study_Hours.

```{r simple-model}
simple_model <- lm(
  Marks ~ Study_Hours,
  data = regression_data
)

summary(simple_model)
```

I look at the coefficients, R-squared, p-value and residual standard error when reading the model summary.

## 5.3 Model coefficients

The intercept is the estimated mark at zero study hours. The slope estimates the change in marks for one additional study hour.

```{r coefficients}
model_coefficients <- coef(simple_model)
model_coefficients
```

## 5.4 Prediction

I used `predict()` to estimate marks for 5, 8 and 12 study hours. The value 12 is outside the observed range, so that prediction is an extrapolation.

```{r simple-prediction}
new_data <- data.frame(Study_Hours = c(5, 8, 12))

predicted_marks <- predict(
  simple_model,
  newdata = new_data
)

data.frame(
  Study_Hours = new_data$Study_Hours,
  Predicted_Marks = as.numeric(predicted_marks)
)
```

## 5.5 Regression graph

The points show the observed values. The line shows the fitted linear relationship.

```{r regression-graph, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(regression_data, aes(x = Study_Hours, y = Marks)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Simple Linear Regression",
    x = "Study Hours",
    y = "Marks"
  )
```

## 5.6 Multiple linear regression

I added Attendance as a second predictor. The plus sign in the formula includes both predictors.

```{r multiple-model}
multiple_model <- lm(
  Marks ~ Study_Hours + Attendance,
  data = regression_data
)

summary(multiple_model)
```

## 5.7 Prediction with two predictors

The new data must contain both predictor columns used in the model.

```{r multiple-prediction}
new_students <- data.frame(
  Study_Hours = c(5, 8),
  Attendance = c(75, 90)
)

multiple_predictions <- predict(
  multiple_model,
  newdata = new_students
)

data.frame(
  new_students,
  Predicted_Marks = as.numeric(multiple_predictions)
)
```

## 5.8 Regression diagnostic plots

I used the four standard plots from `plot(lm_model)`.

1. **Residuals vs Fitted:** checks linearity and whether residual spread is roughly constant.
2. **Normal Q-Q:** checks whether residuals are approximately normal.
3. **Scale-Location:** another check of constant residual spread.
4. **Residuals vs Leverage:** helps identify potentially influential observations.

```{r diagnostic-plots, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(simple_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

These plots do not prove independence. I also need to consider how the observations were collected.

# 6. Debugging in R

Debugging means finding and fixing errors in code.

Common errors I may meet:

- **Syntax error:** code is written incorrectly.
- **Runtime error:** code starts but stops while running.
- **Logical error:** code runs but gives the wrong answer.

## 6.1 RStudio debugging tools

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| Breakpoint | Pauses execution at a selected line |
| Step Into | Moves into a function |
| Step Over | Runs the current line without entering a function |
| Step Out | Finishes the current function and returns to its caller |
| Continue | Resumes execution |
| Environment | Shows current objects and their values |
| Call Stack | Shows the chain of function calls |

## 6.2 traceback()

After an error, `traceback()` displays the function calls that led to it. Run it immediately after the error in the Console.

```{r traceback-example, eval=FALSE}
mean("hello")
traceback()
```

## 6.3 browser()

`browser()` pauses execution inside a function so I can inspect objects. While paused, I can type commands in the Console. Type `c` to continue.

```{r browser-example, eval=FALSE}
debug_example <- function(x) {
  total <- sum(x)
  browser()
  average <- total / length(x)
  return(average)
}

debug_example(c(10, 20, 30))
```

## 6.4 debug(), debugonce() and undebug()

These functions help me step through a function. The following example is not run automatically because it starts an interactive debugging session.

```{r debug-functions, eval=FALSE}
debug(calculate_average)
calculate_average(c(10, 20, 30))
undebug(calculate_average)

debugonce(calculate_average)
calculate_average(c(10, 20, 30))
```

## 6.5 recover()

`recover()` lets me choose a function environment to inspect after an error.

```{r recover-example, eval=FALSE}
options(error = recover)

# Run code that produces an error, then inspect the call stack.
# Return to the normal error behaviour afterwards:
options(error = NULL)
```

## 6.6 try() and tryCatch()

`try()` lets the script continue after an error. `tryCatch()` lets me specify what should happen when an error occurs.

```{r error-handling}
try(log("not a number"))

result <- tryCatch(
  {
    log("not a number")
  },
  error = function(e) {
    message("I found an error: ", e$message)
    NA
  }
)

result
```

## 6.7 stopifnot()

`stopifnot()` checks conditions that should be TRUE. It stops with an error if a condition is FALSE.

```{r stopifnot}
test_values <- c(10, 20, 30)

stopifnot(is.numeric(test_values))
stopifnot(length(test_values) == 3)

"Both checks passed"
```

**What I need to remember:**

- `traceback()` shows calls leading to an error.
- `browser()` pauses code so I can inspect values.
- `debug()` steps through a function.
- `debugonce()` debugs the next call only.
- `undebug()` turns off debugging for a function.
- `recover()` lets me inspect function environments after an error.
- `try()` and `tryCatch()` help handle errors.
- `stopifnot()` checks conditions.
